rubrics.title: Economic History undergraduate marking criteria (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
SCOPE AND APPROACH
The Department's exam marking criteria are benchmarks for timed undergraduate exam essays; similar criteria apply to essays and other assessed work. They are intended as broad guides, for general guidance only: assessing quality is no exact science. In economic history, claims are judged less on whether they are right or wrong than on how well they are supported with well-selected historical evidence. Typical aspects considered are knowledge and understanding, use of literature, argument and analysis, and clarity of expression. No separate dissertation criteria are published (the EH390 dissertation is 10,000 words).

FIRST CLASS (70-100)
90-100: analysis of such originality or insight as potentially to change some aspect of conventional understanding of the subject; for a thesis, work that is potentially publishable.
80-89: analysis of exceptional quality, based on comprehensive knowledge (both historical and conceptual) of the topic, which either develops an original argument in response to the question or shows independent critical discussion and insight.
70-79: analysis which shows both broad and deep knowledge of the historical evidence and conceptual command of the subject; close engagement with the question; an informed grasp of the historical period; and engagement with the issues raised in the historical literature.

UPPER SECOND (60-69)
Clearly written and well-argued work which reflects an understanding of the question as well as the historical period and the issues under discussion; engages seriously with the question, analyses the relevant material thoroughly and recognises its implications.

LOWER SECOND (50-59)
Work which displays an understanding of the questions set and knowledge of the historical periods and issues, but whose critical analysis is less than systematic and whose discussion is not consistently focused on or relevant to the question.

THIRD (40-49)
Work which shows sufficient knowledge to frame a basic answer to the question, with some relevant information on the period and issues, but which lacks clarity and originality, shows weak analytical skills, contains factual inaccuracies and strays from the question.

FAIL (0-39)
34-39: work which provides some material relevant to the question and demonstrates some knowledge of the historical period and issues, but is badly marred by errors, omissions and weak relevance, with very little analytical understanding.
30-33: work which fails to proceed beyond the most rudimentary acquaintance with the historical period and issues; little attention to the precise question; persistent factual errors, or inability to sustain a consistently coherent argument.
20-30: characterised by paucity of information, confusion and lack of relevance, but with some germane points or information.
0-19: work which reveals paucity of information or knowledge about the period and question; persistent confusion and error in the historical ideas discussed; no real engagement with the question or coherent argument; or work that is seriously truncated and totally undeveloped.
(The printed fail sub-bands 20-30 and 30-33 overlap at 30.)

rubrics.title: Economics undergraduate marking criteria (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
SCOPE
The Department of Economics assessment criteria (BSc Handbook) largely relate to formatively assessed classwork and summative examinations; other forms of assessment (e.g. class participation, group work) may use different criteria, which course leaders explain. Exams test and challenge knowledge and understanding rather than repetition of class material, and examiners value evidence of original thought. Each band is described on four aspects: (i) knowledge and understanding of frameworks, techniques and evidence; (ii) choice and application of solution methods; (iii) analytical reasoning (in algebra, diagrams and words); (iv) critical discussion of the limitations of models and the literature; plus an overall judgement.

WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE
A GOOD FIRST (above 75): highly detailed and accurate understanding of frameworks, techniques and evidence; excellent choice and application of an appropriate approach; outstanding analytical reasoning that is precise, economical and clear in analysis, diagrams and words; thorough critical discussion of the limitations of models and literature. Overall: demonstrates outstanding knowledge and skills, with extensive study.

A FIRST (70-75): close to the Good First standard across much of the work but with minor gaps or skipped logical steps; method mostly strong with occasional lapses in detail or in applying the model; reasoning largely excellent with slips in calculation or minor errors in equations; critical discussion broadly correct but sometimes shallow. Overall: outstanding, with some errors or omissions.

B+ 2.1 (60-69): good understanding but with some omissions or less depth and accuracy; an appropriate approach chosen, with some gaps or errors; reasoning sound but sometimes imprecise, diagrams sometimes flawed, occasional unclear or irrelevant verbal points; some relevant critical discussion, with omissions or limited depth. Overall: very good knowledge and skills, comprehensive study.

B 2.2/2.1 (57-59): slightly short of the 2.1 standard: more frequent errors and omissions, or weaker organisation, so material may be conveyed imprecisely.

B 2.2 (50-57): good understanding in several areas but several omissions and errors and thin detail; gaps and errors in method, weaker on the harder later parts of questions or on variants of taught material; reasoning incomplete or imprecise, diagrams incomplete or wrong; limited critical discussion. Overall: good in some areas, partial or superficial in others; restricted ability to transfer methods.

C THIRD (40-49): some understanding but large gaps and errors, incomplete answers; limited method, struggles even with questions close to course material; reasoning weak and often unclear, with missing steps or irrelevant points; little or no critical discussion. Overall: weak knowledge, superficial or partial study.

D FAIL (20-39): minimal understanding and large gaps, with some attempt at some questions; very restricted method; very poor or absent reasoning; critical discussion typically absent. Overall: minimal knowledge or evidence of study.

D BAD FAIL (0-20): very little knowledge or evidence of study; bad fails might not be counted as an attempt.

NOTE
The printed bands overlap at 57 (2.2/2.1 57-59, 2.2 50-57); they are reproduced as published. Class bands for classification follow the School scale (First 70+, 2:1 60-69, 2:2 50-59, Third 40-49).

rubrics.title: Government undergraduate marking criteria (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE (Department of Government Undergraduate Marking Scheme)
FIRST CLASS HONOURS (1), 70-100: a first-class answer will always engage closely with the question and demonstrate distinction in the range and command of material, argument and analysis. Coherent, logical structure; clear, lucid style integrating theory and evidence; draws on a breadth of relevant literature. A first may be awarded on more than one set of criteria: arguments may be sophisticated, fluent and incisive, with exceptional knowledge and possibly an original approach. Within the class, grading depends on sophistication, understanding and originality: 70-74 requires excellence; 75-79 marks outstanding answers; 80 and above is reserved for truly exceptional answers.

UPPER SECOND (2A), 60-69: focuses closely on the question and shows intelligent, broad-based engagement with relevant material. Arguments comprehensive, logically structured, clearly organised and expressed, with wide reference to appropriate literature. Top of band: high ability, superior judgement, prioritisation and sophistication. Bottom of band: still competent, accurate and widely read, but with less depth of understanding or argument.

LOWER SECOND (2B), 50-59: generally competent and broadly relevant but lacking sophistication, depth and focus; limited examples, organisation and breadth of reference; some sections of limited relevance to the main argument; style may be clumsy or unsophisticated. Good answers that stray from the question should normally not be marked above Lower Second. Top of band: reasonably well argued with satisfactory knowledge but unimaginative understanding; answers that would otherwise be 2A but are too short, rushed, unfinished or badly organised. Bottom of band: too much indiscriminate information, factual errors, clumsy prose, or pre-packaged answers only loosely related to the question.

THIRD (3), 40-49: a third-class answer will show little knowledge of the specific issues discussed or their broader context; deficient grasp, understanding and breadth of reference; little sustained argument, poor organisation and expression, key points omitted, inaccuracies. Top of band: a reasonable answer that is unduly brief, poorly organised or includes material largely unrelated to the question. Bottom of band: serious deficiencies in argument, logic, understanding of key issues and style.

FAIL (F), 0-39: work that is seriously deficient in knowledge, understanding and salience; mostly irrelevant; no serious recognition of the question or evidence that course material was understood. Top of band: refers to themes the question anticipates and suggests some understanding but is clearly deficient, superficial or incomplete (e.g. ran out of time). Middle: hints at relevant material but mostly lacks relevance, direction, accuracy and substance. Bottom: no relevant material, negligible understanding, or barely any attempt. Zero may be awarded where the answer is effectively missing or does not engage with the question at all.

PROCESS AND PENALTIES
Summative work is anonymous; each script has an internal marker and a selection is moderated by a second member of staff, with external examiners resolving disagreements; GV390 dissertations are double marked. Recommended over-length deductions: up to 5% over, none; 5-10%, 5 marks; 10-15%, 10; 15-20%, 15; 20-30%, 20; over 30%, 50. Late summative work loses 5 marks per working day.

This is the only Government UG handbook publicly hosted on lse.ac.uk; current handbooks are internal, so the scheme and especially the penalties (LSE has since adopted School-wide late penalty rules) may have changed.

rubrics.title: International History undergraduate marking criteria (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
SCOPE
The Department's undergraduate marking scheme (Class / Marks % / Attributes) applies to examination answers and assessed coursework in International History courses. Courses taught by the Department of International Relations (e.g. for BSc International Relations and History students) are marked under the IR scheme instead.

WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE
FIRST CLASS 80-100: as for 70-80, plus answers that show strong evidence of independent judgement and originality, often drawing on reading well beyond the course reading list.

FIRST CLASS 70-80: exceptional answers, well presented and argued with sophistication, demonstrating a wide familiarity with the subject matter and the historiographical debate.

2.1 60-69: competent work showing a good grasp of the subject matter. Evidence of familiarity with the most important reading and historiographical debates; factually correct and fairly comprehensive in coverage, though there may be minor slips; clearly organised and addressing the question directly; relevant terms and concepts understood and used correctly.

2.2 50-59: answers demonstrate some understanding of the subject matter but are marred by poor presentation or by lack of sophisticated argument or knowledge. Often narrative in style and addressing the question only indirectly or inadequately; may contain unsupported generalisations, occasional inaccuracies, irrelevance, omissions and contradictions. The main issues are understood but treated superficially, with little that goes beyond the standard reading.

3RD CLASS 40-49: weak answers which nevertheless show evidence that there is some familiarity with the subject. Mainly weak narrative or descriptive accounts that move towards the area required by the question but show only a partial grasp of the topic and of the question; argument fleeting and often simplistic; basic familiarity with the facts alongside inaccuracies and omissions.

FAIL 30-39: incoherent and poorly structured answers containing many errors and showing little knowledge of the subject matter; also coherent and adequately structured answers that wholly fail to address the question.

FAIL 0-29: minimal evidence of any familiarity with the subject matter, combined with failure to address the question and incoherent structure and argument.

MARKING PROCESS
Each script or essay is read and marked by one examiner under a moderated marking scheme. A moderator checks a proportion of scripts, including fails, borderline marks and firsts; an external examiner reviews a sample; marks are agreed at Sub-Boards of Examiners, and marking is anonymous until grades are confirmed. The dissertation is 10,000 words and counts as one paper; gobbet answers are limited to one or two sides of A4.
rubrics.source_note: LSE Department of International History, Undergraduate Handbook 2026-27: undergraduate marking scheme (pp.57-58), marking process (p.55), dissertation and gobbets (pp.50, 54). Earlier editions: 2024-25 (https://www.lse.ac.uk/International-History/Assets/Documents/student-handbooks/2024-25/24-0180-UG-IH-handbook-v3.1.pdf) and 2023-24.

rubrics.title: International Relations undergraduate marking criteria (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
SCOPE AND APPROACH
Courses taught by the Department of International Relations are examined and marked according to criteria set out in its undergraduate marking scheme. The scheme notes that writing essays and examination answers is a creative process; in International Relations there are no straightforwardly correct answers, and most work mixes strengths and weaknesses, so class-teacher feedback is key. Each band is described on six criteria: relevance to the question; structure and organisation; clarity of exposition; analysis and argument; knowledge and understanding of evidence, concepts and debates in the literature (and reading); referencing/bibliography.

WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE
OUTSTANDING (FIRST CLASS) 80+: wholly relevant to the question; very good structure and organisation, all building to support the persuasiveness of the conclusion; excellent exposition of evidence, concepts and arguments, well written; excellent, original analysis and argument; excellent knowledge and understanding of evidence, concepts and debates in the literature, demonstrating wide reading; good referencing/bibliography.

EXCELLENT (FIRST CLASS) 70-79: as for 80+ in relevance, structure, exposition, knowledge and referencing, but with strong analysis and independently formulated argument (rather than excellent, original analysis).

VERY GOOD (UPPER SECOND) 60-69: wholly relevant to the question; good structure and organisation supporting a clear conclusion; strong exposition of evidence, concepts and arguments, well written; good analysis and independent argument; very good knowledge and understanding of evidence, concepts and debates, showing essential and wider reading; good referencing/bibliography.

GOOD (LOWER SECOND) 50-59: predominantly relevant to the question; satisfactory structure and organisation, clear conclusion; clear exposition of evidence, concepts and arguments, reasonably clearly written; some good analysis and argument, some weak analysis and argument; good but partial knowledge and understanding of evidence, concepts and debates, with evidence of essential and some wider reading; good referencing/bibliography.

ADEQUATE (THIRD CLASS HONOURS) 40-49: partial relevance to the question; satisfactory structure; underdeveloped analysis and argument; adequate referencing/bibliography.

UNSATISFACTORY (FAIL) 20-39: poorly focused on the question; poor structure and organisation, not supporting the conclusion; poor clarity of exposition, badly written; lack of analysis, poor argument; basic knowledge and/or understanding, limited evidence of essential reading; poor referencing/bibliography.

VERY UNSATISFACTORY (BAD FAIL) 0-19: irrelevant to the question; absence of structure/organisation, no or unsupported conclusion; unclear exposition, badly written; no analysis or argument; no knowledge and/or understanding of evidence, concepts or debates in the literature; no or very poor referencing/bibliography.
rubrics.source_note: Department of International Relations undergraduate marking scheme as reproduced in the LSE Department of International History Undergraduate Handbook 2026-27 (pp.59-60), in the BSc International Relations and History section. The IR department's own UG handbook is not public (its assessments page, https://www.lse.ac.uk/international-relations/current-students/key-information/assessments-and-exams, points to Moodle). The Third-class row was only partly extractable (exposition and knowledge descriptors missing).

rubrics.title: Law (LLB) undergraduate classification scheme (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
WHAT IS PUBLISHED
LSE Law School does not publish qualitative undergraduate marking criteria or grade descriptors on its public site (handbooks and course criteria are on Moodle). What is published is the LLB's own classification scheme, which differs from the School's BA/BSc scheme and is condensed here.

MARK BANDS (LLB, students entering 2024/25)
70-100 First
60-69 Upper Second
50-59 Lower Second
45-49 Third
40-44 Pass
Below 40 Fail. In Year One, 30-39 is a Fail and 0-29 a Bad Fail.
Note the LLB has a separate Pass band (40-44) and a narrower Third (45-49) than the BA/BSc scale.

WHICH MARKS COUNT
Only Years Two and Three count. Each half unit is one classification mark and each full unit counts twice, giving sixteen classification marks; the aggregate is their sum. The latest attempt at each course is used. For candidates registered from 2011/12, a first-class mark in a non-Law course is capped at 73 when calculating the aggregate.

HOW THE CLASS IS DETERMINED
First: eight first-class marks; or six first-class marks and an aggregate within 10 of the normal aggregate of 1080.
Upper Second: eight upper-second marks or above; or six and an aggregate within 10 of 960.
Lower Second: eight lower-second marks or above; or six and an aggregate within 10 of 800.
Third: eight third-class marks or above; or six and an aggregate within 10 of 720.
Pass: sixteen pass marks or above; or twelve pass marks or above including at least two third-class or above, with a normal aggregate of 640.
Penalty: two failed classification marks drop the award by one class (not applied where an overall Pass is awarded).

ATTEMPTS, PROGRESSION AND RESITS
Three attempts are allowed in each year; not attempting without an approved deferral counts as an attempt. Year One: every element must be attempted; failing 1.0 unit allows progression with a resit; failing 2.0 or more units, or scoring below 30 in 1.0 or more units, fails the year; Year One resit marks are not capped. Year Two progression requires seven passes with the failed mark at least 30, six passes with failed marks at least 35, or four passes with failed marks at least 38. Year Three: a candidate passes if all courses are passed, or at least six classification marks are passed with at least 30 in each failed course. Passed resits in Years Two and Three are capped at 40 for classification and aggregate. A passed assessment cannot be resat.

EXCEPTIONAL CIRCUMSTANCES
The Board may depart from the scheme only on a formal submission, where circumstances were sudden, unforeseen and outside the student's control, the student is within 3 marks of the next boundary, has marks in the higher range, and performance was significantly out of line with unaffected assessments.

Linked from the LSE Calendar 2026-27 undergraduate page. A 2023/24-entry scheme is also published (SchemeBachelorOfLaws2023.pdf). No public LSE Law School UG marking criteria or grade descriptors were found.

rubrics.title: Mathematics undergraduate marking criteria (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
SCOPE
The Department's Assessment Criteria give broad descriptors for examination marks. Its undergraduate courses conform to the QAA Subject Benchmark Statement for Mathematics, Statistics and Operational Research. Exams test understanding and problem-solving; revision lectures indicate what is expected. Homework is graded by class teachers mainly as feedback (in some courses it contributes 10% of the course grade for consistent effort).

WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE
90-100 FIRST CLASS: a comprehensive and deep understanding of the subject; mastery of relevant methods and techniques and an ability to deploy them with flair; very extensive range and consistent accuracy of information and knowledge; an outstanding ability to solve unusual and demanding questions involving application of deep and comprehensive understanding of the subject and its methods.

80-89 FIRST CLASS: a deep understanding of the subject; mastery of relevant methods and techniques; highly extensive range and consistent accuracy of information and knowledge; an impressive ability to solve more unusual or demanding questions involving application of deep understanding of the subject and its methods.

70-79 FIRST CLASS: a thorough understanding of the subject; deft application of relevant methods and techniques; extensive range and consistent accuracy of information and knowledge; a significant capacity to solve more unusual or demanding questions involving application of thorough understanding of the subject and its methods.

60-69 UPPER SECOND CLASS: a clear understanding of the subject; competent application of relevant methods and techniques; wide and accurate range of information and knowledge deployed; some capacity to solve more unusual or demanding questions involving application of significant understanding of the subject.

50-59 LOWER SECOND CLASS: a sound understanding of the subject; knowledge of, and some application of, relevant methods and techniques; a standard, and largely accurate, range of information and knowledge deployed; may demonstrate ability to grapple with standard problems, but limited capacity to solve more unusual or demanding questions involving application of significant understanding of the subject.

40-49 THIRD CLASS: an acceptable demonstration of a basic understanding of and competence in the subject; some knowledge of, and application of, relevant methods and techniques; a basic range of information and knowledge deployed, with some areas of inaccuracy.

30-39 FAIL: some understanding evident, but no ability to grapple with anything other than a limited range of very routine questions; limited competence in core basic techniques of the subject, or competence only in a small part of the material.

20-29 FAIL: little understanding evident; very limited competence in core basic techniques of the subject.

10-19 BAD FAIL: very little information, or information that is almost entirely incorrect or irrelevant; very little evidence of understanding; very little competence in core basic techniques.

1-9 BAD FAIL: nothing presented, or completely incorrect information, or answers containing nothing at all of relevance; no evidence of understanding; no competence in core basic techniques of the subject.

rubrics.title: Social Policy undergraduate marking criteria (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
HOW WORK IS JUDGED
The Department's BSc marking framework is 'a guide to the principal criteria used for the marking of both assessed and formative written work'. Markers comment under four criteria: (1) quality of expression, structure and clarity of argument; (2) awareness and use of literature; (3) knowledge base and understanding; (4) argument and critical analysis. The overall mark reflects an overall judgement based on all four criteria and on the extent to which the student has substantively answered the question(s) set. Individual courses may post tailored frameworks on Moodle.

WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE
I 80+: Exceptionally well-rounded argument; persuasively written. Excellent use of extensive literature well beyond the reading list, impressively exploited. Excellent understanding and outstanding exposition of relevant issues; exceptionally well informed; insightful awareness of nuances and complexities; no major room for improvement given the constraints of the essay form. Argument marshalled in an outstanding manner with excellent integration of theory/conceptual framework; searching questioning, unbiased approach; unambiguous evidence of original and independent thought.

I 70-79: Excellent, logically developed argument; very well written. Very good use of a wide range of literature to support the argument. Very good understanding and exposition of relevant issues; well informed; good awareness of nuances and complexities. Well-constructed arguments with appropriate use of theory/conceptual framework; questioning, unbiased approach; clear evidence of independent thought and of originality.

II.i 60-69: Well-developed argument; well expressed. Good use of a wide range of literature to support arguments. Clear awareness and exposition of relevant issues; some awareness of nuances and complexities but a tendency to simplify matters. High standard of critical analysis with appropriate choice and use of theory/conceptual framework; some questioning of the literature.

II.ii 50-59: Adequately presented argument; meaning generally clear. Adequate use of standard literature to support arguments. Shows understanding of the issue but at a superficial level; no more than expected from attendance at lectures; some irrelevant material. Appropriate choice and use of theory/conceptual framework; attempts analysis.

III 40-49: Confusingly structured and argued; meaning unclear. Use of a narrow range of standard literature. Establishes some relevant points but superficial and confused; much irrelevant material. Weak understanding or use of chosen theory/conceptual framework; too descriptive and/or analysis too superficial.

FAIL below 40: Lacking structure and meaningful argument; difficult to understand. No significant reference to literature. Very little or no understanding of the issues, or topic misunderstood; content largely irrelevant. No choice or use of theory/conceptual framework; almost wholly descriptive; no grasp of analysis, with many errors and/or omissions.
Marks below 30 signify work that is significantly flawed or seriously inadequate; marks below 15 signify only a minimal or no serious attempt.

PROCESS
Text beyond the stated word limit is not considered by markers. Courses use double-blind marking, sighted double marking, or single marking with moderation of a sample; external examiners review a representative sample from each course.

rubrics.title: Sociology undergraduate marking criteria (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
SCOPE
The Department's general Undergraduate Mark Frame illustrates the assessment criteria that markers employ for BSc summative assessments. Where a summative assessment has its own criteria, these are published on the course Moodle page. Degrees are classified under LSE's BSc classification scheme. Written coursework is marked by two internal examiners and moderated by an external examiner; each summative piece receives qualitative comments and an indicative mark.

WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE
FIRST CLASS HONOURS (70-100%): awarded when the assessment demonstrates clarity of analysis, engages directly with the question and shows an independent and critical interpretation of the issues raised by it; shows exemplary skill in presenting a logical and coherent argument; reflects an outstanding breadth and depth of reading; is presented in a polished manner, with all citations, footnotes and bibliography rendered in the proper academic form. Answers in the upper range (above 80%) will be outstanding in terms of originality, sophistication and breadth of understanding of relevant themes and material.

UPPER SECOND CLASS HONOURS (60-69%): awarded when the assessment attempts a systematic analysis of the issues raised by the question; demonstrates independent thought; shows appropriate skill in presenting a clearly reasoned argument; draws on a good range of relevant literature; is well presented, with citations, footnotes and bibliography rendered in the proper academic form.

LOWER SECOND CLASS HONOURS (50-59%): awarded when the assessment shows an understanding of the issues raised by the question and demonstrates some engagement with relevant literature. The discussion may rely more heavily on description than on independent analysis; there may be some inconsistencies, irrelevant points and unsubstantiated claims in the argument. Presentation and referencing are adequate but may contain inaccuracies.

THIRD CLASS HONOURS (40-49%): awarded when the assessment shows a limited understanding of the question, demonstrates a partial familiarity with the issues raised by it, contains a minimal attempt at analysis and argumentation, and demonstrates limited knowledge of the relevant literature. Presentation may be poor and referencing incomplete.

FAIL (20-39%): the assessment shows little understanding of the subject and does not adequately address the question. It may be based entirely on lecture material, poorly structured, and contain significant errors of fact; it may be poorly presented with inadequate referencing and fail to demonstrate knowledge of the relevant literature.

BAD FAIL (0-19%): awarded to assessments that demonstrate no understanding of the question nor of the relevant literature. The assessment may be incomplete and is likely to be poorly presented with little or no referencing.
rubrics.source_note: LSE Department of Sociology 'Undergraduate Mark Frame' (undated PDF), identified as the Department's 'BSc marking criteria used by markers for summative assessments' on its Assessment and feedback page (https://lse.ac.uk/sociology/study/assessment-and-feedback). Marking process from the Sociology BSc Student Handbook 2025-26, p.13: https://www.lse.ac.uk/sociology/assets/documents/study/handbooks/Sociology-BSc-Student-Handbook-2025-26.pdf

rubrics.title: Statistics undergraduate marking criteria (London School of Economics and Political Science)
rubrics.body:
MARK SCALE
70% and over First Class; 60-69% Upper Second Class; 50-59% Lower Second Class; 40-49% Third Class; 0-39% Fail.

GENERAL ASSESSMENT CRITERIA FOR EXAMINATIONS
Examinations are assessed on the ability to: (1) know and understand basic concepts and principles; (2) apply knowledge to frame a problem mathematically or statistically; (3) apply core concepts to solve problems, choosing suitable methods and techniques; (4) use mathematical notation accurately; (5) make logical arguments; (6) interpret results and set them in context.

WHAT EACH BAND LOOKS LIKE
FIRST (70-100): thorough and wide-ranging knowledge and understanding; confident application of knowledge, methods and techniques; consistently high level of accuracy; clear and logical arguments; in-depth interpretation of results; significant capacity to solve more demanding questions requiring non-standard application of knowledge.

2:1 (60-69): clear knowledge and understanding; competent application of methods and techniques; high level of accuracy; largely clear and logical arguments; appropriate interpretation of results; some capacity to solve more demanding questions requiring non-standard application of knowledge.

2:2 (50-59): sound knowledge and understanding; application of knowledge to standard problems; largely accurate; generally clear arguments; largely appropriate but sometimes cursory interpretation of results; limited capacity to solve more demanding questions.

THIRD (40-49): acceptable knowledge of the subject, but gaps in understanding; basic competence in applying knowledge to standard problems; a number of slips in accuracy; arguments sometimes poorly expressed; cursory interpretation of results; little capacity to solve demanding questions.

FAIL (0-39): little evidence of knowledge, understanding or the ability to apply it to solve problems; a large number of errors; poorly expressed arguments; little attempt at interpretation of results, or inappropriate interpretation.

HOW EXAMS ARE MARKED
Questions may be broken down into smaller steps and marked step by step, so the final mark reflects the proportion of parts answered correctly; the principle of partial credit is observed as far as feasible. Marks are approved by a second examiner but remain provisional until confirmed by the Sub-Board of Examiners. Assessment criteria for coursework are course-specific and provided by the course leader.

LATE PENALTIES
Five marks per half-day (or part) late in the first 24 hours, capped at ten marks; thereafter five marks per further 24-hour period; for assessments set over more than three weeks, five marks per day. Extensions only in exceptional circumstances, approved by the Exam Board Chair.
